text: Merleau-Ponty uses the brain-injured patient Schneider — who could perform concrete purposive movements but not abstract ones out of context — to illustrate:
choices: That perception is the passive reception of sense-data (empiricism)
That action is the execution of explicit mental representations (intellectualism)
Motor intentionality as a distinct, pre-reflective bodily directedness
The reduction of the lived body to the objective body of physiology
explanation: Schneider's selective deficit — neither purely motor nor purely intellectual — reveals motor intentionality as a third, pre-reflective dimension of bodily directedness. Merleau-Ponty invokes the case precisely to reject both empiricism (passive sensation) and intellectualism (explicit representation), and not to reduce the lived body to the objective body.
